title: UI vs UX design
summary: UI is the visual and interactive surface (layout, type, colour, controls); UX is the whole experience of reaching a goal with a product, before, during and after the screen. A product can have a polished UI and a poor UX. Roles: UI designer, UX researcher, interaction designer.
emphasis: For the 2-mark difference question, give one line each plus one concrete example (e.g. a beautiful app whose checkout takes 9 taps). Definitions alone get 1 mark.

title: Core stages of design thinking
summary: Empathize (understand users through observation and interviews), Define (frame the problem as a user need), Ideate (generate many solutions), Prototype (cheap, testable artefacts), Test (learn from users and iterate). The process is non-linear: testing loops back to define and ideate.
emphasis: Draw the five stages as a loop with arrows going back - a straight line of five boxes loses the diagram mark for iteration.

title: Divergent and convergent thinking
summary: Divergent thinking widens the option space (quantity, no judgement); convergent thinking narrows it using criteria (impact, feasibility, cost). The double-diamond shape alternates the two. Tools for converging: dot voting, impact/effort matrix.
emphasis: In any ideation answer, show BOTH: list several ideas, then state the criteria you used to pick one. Picking an idea with no criteria loses the justification marks.

title: Brainstorming and gamestorming
summary: Brainstorming rules: defer judgement, go for quantity, build on others' ideas, one conversation at a time. Gamestorming: structured games for opening, exploring and closing (e.g. Crazy 8s, empathy map game, dot voting, 2x2 matrix).
emphasis: Name the specific game and say what phase it serves (open, explore, close).

title: Observational empathy and empathy maps
summary: Observe users in context without leading them: what they do, workarounds, pain points. Empathy map quadrants: Says, Thinks, Does, Feels, plus Pains and Gains. Observation reveals what users do, interviews reveal what they say - the gap is the insight.
emphasis: An empathy map must be filled with scenario-specific entries in all four quadrants. An empty template diagram earns nothing.

title: Workshop: design thinking on the campus canteen
summary: Applied all five stages to the LICET canteen lunch rush. Observed the queue, built an empathy map, wrote a POV statement, ran HMW questions, sketched a paper prototype of a pre-order and pickup-slot flow, and planned a 5-student test. POV format: [user] needs [need] because [insight].
emphasis: The Define stage must state a USER NEED, not a solution. 'The canteen needs an app' is a solution and gets 0 for Define. Answers that only define the five stages without applying them to the scenario are capped at about 4/10.

title: Tutorial: writing Unit 1 application answers
summary: Practised 10-mark answers: restate the scenario and users, draw the process, apply each stage with specific evidence, justify the chosen idea, end with how you would test and iterate.
emphasis: Last batch lost an average of 3 marks per application question by writing textbook theory and never mentioning the scenario again.

title: Visual and UI principles
summary: Visual hierarchy (size, weight, colour, position), contrast, alignment, proximity, repetition, white space, and the Gestalt principles (proximity, similarity, closure, continuity, figure-ground).
emphasis: Each principle needs a named on-screen example ('the Pay button is the only filled button, so it leads the hierarchy'). Principles listed without examples get half marks.

title: UI elements and patterns
summary: Input controls, navigational components (tab bar, hamburger, breadcrumbs), informational components (toasts, badges, progress), containers (cards, modals). Patterns as reusable solutions: onboarding, empty states, search with filters.
emphasis: Say WHEN to use a pattern, not just what it is - e.g. tab bar for 3-5 top-level destinations on mobile.

title: Interaction behaviours and principles
summary: Affordance and signifiers, feedback, consistency, constraints, mapping. Fitts's law: time to reach a target depends on distance and size - make primary targets big and close. Hick's law: decision time grows with the number of choices - reduce and group options.
emphasis: State the law, then apply it to a screen. Fitts's law with no design consequence gets 1 of 2 marks.

title: Branding in UI
summary: Brand attributes translated into colour, typography, imagery, iconography, voice and tone. Consistency across touchpoints builds recognition and trust.
emphasis: Connect each visual choice to a brand attribute ('rounded type for a friendly fest brand').

title: Style guides and design systems
summary: A style guide documents colour palette with roles, type scale, spacing grid, components with states (default, hover, disabled, error), iconography, and voice. A design system adds coded components and usage rules.
emphasis: Components must be shown with their states. A colour list without roles (primary, error, surface) loses marks.

title: Critique session: the college fee-payment page
summary: Critiqued the fee-payment page using visual principles and interaction laws: weak hierarchy, three equally loud buttons, tiny tap targets, no feedback after payment.
emphasis: Critique format: observation -> principle violated -> impact on the user -> fix. Use this four-part structure in the exam.

title: IA1 revision and marking scheme
summary: Shared the IA1 marking scheme for 10-mark application questions: scenario and users 1, diagram or visual artefact 2, concepts named and explained 2, application to the scenario 3, justification and next step 2.
emphasis: The application criterion (3 marks) is where most marks are lost. Every concept you name must be tied to the given scenario.

title: Introduction to UX; the UX honeycomb
summary: Why UX matters: adoption, retention, support cost, accessibility. Morville's UX honeycomb: useful, usable, desirable, findable, accessible, credible, valuable.
emphasis: The honeycomb is a sure 2-mark question. For 10 marks, evaluate a real product against all seven facets.

title: The UX design process: double diamond
summary: Discover (research), Define (synthesise into a problem), Develop (ideate and prototype), Deliver (test, refine, ship). Each diamond diverges then converges. Mapped to design thinking stages.
emphasis: Draw both diamonds with labels on all four phases and mark where divergence and convergence happen.

title: UX research methods and tools
summary: Qualitative vs quantitative; attitudinal vs behavioural. Interviews, surveys, contextual inquiry, diary studies, analytics, competitive analysis. Tools: interview guides, screeners, affinity mapping, survey forms.
emphasis: Most likely IA2 10-marker: pick methods for a given product AND justify each choice by what it reveals. A list of methods without justification gets at most 4/10.

title: User needs and goals
summary: Needs vs wants; goals at three levels (experience, end, life goals). Jobs to be done: 'When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome]'.
emphasis: Write at least one goal in the JTBD format for the given user.

title: Business goals and user goals
summary: Business goals (revenue, retention, cost reduction) expressed as KPIs. Conflicts with user goals (dark patterns, forced sign-up). Resolution: find overlap, measure both, choose designs that serve the user and the metric.
emphasis: Give one concrete conflict and one concrete resolution with a metric. Generic 'balance both' gets no application marks.

title: Case study: a food-delivery app
summary: Walked through research planning for a food-delivery app: interviews with hostel students, analytics on cart abandonment, survey on delivery-time expectations; mapped user goals against the business goal of order frequency.
emphasis: Use a table in the exam: method | why | what it reveals. Tables earn the visual artefact marks for research questions.

title: Sketching principles and red routes
summary: Sketch fast and rough; quantity over polish; annotate. Red routes: the critical, frequent paths users must complete (e.g. pay fees, download hall ticket) - design and test these first.
emphasis: Identify the red route of the given product before sketching anything.

title: Responsive design
summary: Fluid grids, flexible images, breakpoints, mobile-first. Content priority changes across sizes; navigation collapses; touch targets of at least 44-48 px.
emphasis: Show the same screen at two breakpoints and say what moves, hides or stacks.

title: Wireframing and wireflows
summary: Low-fidelity wireframes show structure and content priority, not visual style. Wireflows combine wireframes with arrows showing the interaction that moves the user between screens.
emphasis: Classic IA2 10-marker: wireframe 3-4 screens of a red route and connect them with labelled arrows. Unlabelled arrows lose the flow marks.

title: Lab: high-fidelity prototyping in Figma
summary: Built a clickable high-fidelity prototype in Figma using components, auto layout and prototype links.
emphasis: Figma prototyping is assessed in the lab record only - it will NOT be asked in the IA2 written paper.
